speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, March 29, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) for committee of supply, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Guthrie.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it is possible that in the course of my remarks I may disagree rather strongly with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) with respect to some points of his address of yesterday and the amendment which followed it, I am pleased to preface my remarks by congratulating him on the tone of his address. Indeed the form deserved commendation more than the substance. I am pleased also to say that I agree ' with him at least on the first statement which he made as to the nature and functions of the Imperial conference, a statement which should dispel much misconception in that regard.
The Imperial conference is not an executive, nor a government, nor a cabinet; it is a consultative body and nothing else. That was the position taken by all prime ministers of Canada in the past and by those of the other dominions of the empire as well. It is a consultative body composed of representatives of the various units of the empire who meet, get each other's opinions, discuss conditions and problems which affect all or some of them, and, in the light of knowledge and impressions received and communicated to them, may afterwards if necessary recommeml to thei*

1702	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
respective parliaments any legislation, or executive act which may best suit the need.
To assert that the Imperial conference may change the constitution of Canada or the constitution of any other dominion is an absurdity. The conference has no power to do that and it could not undertake to do it. There was formerly throughout the British Empire a school of opinion favouring a sort of imperial federation or the creation of a central body representing all parts of the empire and having executive duties and powers. This scheme has been rejected by the overwhelming will of the peoples of the empire. We would never accept it in Canada; we would never agree that problems affecting Canada should be decided by a body in which Canada would be submerged and in the minority, and where decisions would be reached by a majority composed of friendly people, if you will, but friendly outsiders.
But if we do not want a central body with executive powers over all the nations of the empire, we also do not want disruption. We want to preserve as much as possible the association of the nations of the commonwealth, and the Imperial conference is one of the means of preserving if possible this association by promoting friendly meetings, friendly discussions of problems, and friendly intercourse. I repeat: The Imperial conference of 1926, no more than Imperial conferences of the past, could not alter or change one iota of the British North America Act or the constitution of any other part of the empire. What the conference could do and did was to affirm, to reaffirm, principles which have gradually come to establish themselves very firmly in place of other principles which governed in the past with regard to the status of the nations of the empire, and to call attention to certain usages, conventions, or practices which may not altogether harmonize with the adopted principle of equality of status of all the nations of the commonwealth.
These premises being laid, I state, whatever may be said to the contrary, that the achievements of the conference of 1926 and the spirit of cooperation which alone could make them possible, make it an historical event in the history of the British commonwealth of nations. The conference has crystallized the principle of equality of status which was already recognized and which was the logical outcome of the development of the various nations. It has published a definite, clear and

official adherence to that principle. It has done so in such a way as to make it the greatest contribution to the permanency of the free association of the nations of the commonwealth. It is the final and unequivocal acceptance of the principle of unity and liberty, unity preserved and enshrined in the British throne, and liberty in all domestic and external activities of the various nations of the commonwealth. It is no longer, as has been said by some writer, the case of "daughter am I in my mother's house, but mistress in my own". The family is a family of sisters equal in their rights and activities.
It is a magnificent tribute to the broadmindedness, wisdom and statesmanship of the public men of Britain that they have unequivocally accepted this great principle that the foundation of the commonwealth rests upon the solid rock of liberty, economy and equality of the various parts thereof. It is stated in the report that such a tendency was both right and inevitable. In this they do not agree with some Canadian newspapermen, but I think their opinion is more free from bias and political partisanship than those of our contradictors on this side of the ocean. May I say that I have been surprised to find that some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House and their supporters in the press have taken exception to the principle of equality of status and equality of nationhood.
Mr. McGIBBON Mr. LAPOINTE Mr. McGIBBON
No.
Who says no? I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will
take the Hansard of this session and read the speech of his leader, he will see that although my hon. friend the leader of the opposition yesterday changed to some extent his line of attack and is now hanging his amendment upon a sentence of the Imperial conference report concerning the Privy Council, he did not do so in his speech on the address. Then it was equality of status that was harmful and dangerous for the minority in this country. The press of Canada supporting my hon. friends opposite are not agreed among themselves, because there are two schools of critics, one claiming that no change has been made, and the other claiming that a terrible and a dangerous change has been made. To the first school I say that if the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
dominions were satisfied to accept their views in the matter, then, to use the language of a great British writer, they would not be worthy of the stock from which they sprang. But it is not the assertion of a new doctrine, and my friend the leader of the opposition has seen to some extent the error of his ways in that respect, for in his address yesterday he said that he agreed with the principle of equality of status. Still, I want to set the matter right before the Canadian people. I want to show that it was not a new principle which was crystallized, if you will, in the report of the conference, but a principle to which adhesion had been given in the past, and especially during the last ten years, by the public men of Canada both in this House of Commons and elsewhere. I shall not quote the words of my late lamented leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I wish to quote the words of writers or speakers friendly to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. Let me first quote from the memorandum which Sir Robert Borden circulated on behalf of the prime ministers of the dominions in March, 1919, when the present leader of the opposition was a member of his government:
All the treaties and conventions resulting from the Peace conference should be so drafted as to enable the dominions to become parties and signatories thereto. This procedure will give suitable recognition to the part played at the peace table by the British commonwealth as a whole, and will, at the same time, record the status attained there by the dominions. The procedure is in consonance with the principles of constitutional government that obtain throughout the empire. The crown is the supreme executive in the United Kingdom and in all the dominions, but it acts on the advice of different ministries within different constitutional units; and under resolution IX of the Imperial War conference, 1917 the organization of the empire is to be based upon equality of nationhood.
The leader of the opposition, as I said, was a member of the Canadian government at that time. He is responsible for the doctrine asserted in that document, but I do not remember that he submitted it to the House of Commons either before or after that document was circulated. It goes on:
It was the reiteration of the principle laid down by the Imperial War conference of 1917, which stated in their resolution, "that any readjustment should be based upon a full recognition of the dominions as autonomous nations of the imperial commonwealth."
The word "autonomous" did not seem to agree with my hon. friend the leader of the opposition yesterday-

speechtext: Oh yes, it did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Very well. May I also quote from the despatch sent on December 4, 1918, by the government of Canada to the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, Prime Minister, then in London. The government here, of which my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was then a member, was afraid that even Sir Robert Borden would not go far enough then, and they sent him a telegram reading as follows:
Council to-day further considered Canadian representation at Peace conference and is even more strongly of opinion than when you left that Canada should be represented. Council is of opinion that in view of war efforts of Dominion other nations entitled to representation at conference should recognize unique character of British commonwealth composed of group of free nations under one sovereign and that provision should be made for special representation of these nations at conference even though it may be necessary that in any final decisions reached they should speak with one voice. That if this is not possible you should form one of whatever delegation represents British commonwealth.
Those of us who had the privilege of being members of the House of Commons in 1919 will remember the pride with which the members of the then administration spoke in the House of Commons of the tremendous step forward they had achieved in acquiring equality of nationhood for Canada in the British commonwealth, and they were rather abusive of the members of this House who did not see exactly eye to eye with them in the matter. The then Minister of Justice asserted, in the name of the government, Canada's absolute right constitutionally to govern herself in accordance with the laws made by the parliament of Canada. Listen to his words:
It has not been claimed on this side of the House that this treaty made Canada a nation; nor has it been claimed that anything that happened at the Peace conference made Canada a nation. Canada has grown to nationhood and Canada is a nation; and she does not go seeking anywhere to any of the allied or associated powers, to any foreign power, to Great Britain herself, to the entire Peace conference, to con-
1704	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
fer upon her the gift of nationhood. Peoples, starting under the tutelage of other countries that have sent forth their sons to establish colonies, in the course of time, as they grow, come to acquire qualities that belong to no colony. What is the proper position of a colony as towards its mother country? Why, it is the position of a child in the nursery. It takes the directions of its mother country: it follows the mother country without any question in whatever line of action that mother country chooses to adopt as governing its conduct towards the outside nations of the world. And when that line of conduct leads to conditions that call for the facing of those outside nations in arms, while the relationship is purely that of guiding and governing mother country and dependent colony, then it is the business of the mother country to provide not only for her own defence, but to carry upon her own shoulders the burden that may result from the line of conduct which she and she alone has chosen to adopt; and if her child colony over there, that had nothing to say about how those conditions were brought about, is exposed to danger, it is for the mother country to defend it. Was that the situation in regard to Canada? Nationhood is a matter of fact; it is not a question of what is written in a statute book or what is declared by one nation in relation to another.
Mr. MANION; Whom is the minister quoting?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
The then Minister of
Justice, the Right Hon. C. J. Doherty. But he used even stronger language. At page 196 of Hansard, 1919, he said-and these words have much bearing on the present debate:
As regards the constitutional question the hon. gentleman has told us, and a number of others have also stated, that we have a written constitution and that that is the last word. We have a written constitution enacted for what purpose? It was enacted to distribute throughout this federal country the powers of legislation. The Privy Council is on record as having said that the whole field of legislation had been by that act conferred upon the Dominion of Canada, either upon its central parliament or upon the parliaments of its provinces. When that was done the last work that a written constitution could do was done. But because we had that written constitution we did not cease to live under that British constitution that is not written in books, that rests upon the continued practice of the British people-of the people of the British Empire, which includes us Canadians as well as the people of the United Kingdom. I was surprised the other evening to hear the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) say that the British constitution was limited to the United Kingdom, as though we had not all of us for years boasted-and no man did it more frequently nor more eloquently than the late leader of the Liberal party-of our enjoying all the benefits and advantages of the British constitution-and it is not all written in the British North America Act.
I do not want to read it all, but I will simply quote the last words:

I have referred to the recent discussion with regard to the aviation law. Over in Great Brtiain they recognize our national status and that constitutionally the whole field of government of Canada is ours. It is only in this country that you find the little man who. wants to hang on to the colonial status of his country and to insist that she is subordinate to and to be governed by another portion of the empire. However great that portion may be-and we all respect it, we all recognize what she was the source of for us all, and we shall all be happy to recognize her as the first among these equal nations-we contend that, ps a matter of fact, we stand as an equal nation within the empire.
The then President of the Privy Council, Mr. Rowell, and the Minister of the Interior, who was then Mr. M-eighen spoke along the same lines and defended the same principle. I suppose that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was in accord with them at the time. In 1921 the Prime Minister of Canada, in one of his speeches published in a book entitled Overseas Addresses, at page 15, says:
We legislate each for ourselves unfettered; we advise through separate councils a common sovereign; we confer together in order to better understand the wider over-riding common interest; between a sense of independence and a sense of unity there is no clash but harmony. On these principles our own league of nations has survived, and it has served the world wonderfully well.
Mr. Meighen, during the same debate said -and I find his words in Sir Robert Borden's book Canadian Constitutional Studies, pages 113 and 114In May 1921, the Canadian Prime Minister-
In the Manchester Guardian centenary number, May 5, 1921
-declared that the relations between the constituent parts of the empire must be based upon a conception of complete freedom and equality in national status. Further he observed that the practical need would be met by clearly understood and definitely accepted declarations of principle with improvements in so much of the form and content of the existing mechanism as may be found to be obsolete.
I could quote numerous words of Sir Robert Borden, especially in his book on constitutional studies, but I suppose it is useless for me to do so. The same doctrine was preached and expounded by all the statesmen of the other dominions, and may I especially mention Mr. Hughes of Australia and General Smuts of South Africa, and they were accepted by the Prime Minister and the various public men of Britain. I have quotations here from Lord Milner, Mr. Amery and Mr. Lloyd George but I would not like to trouble the House by reading them. Never did my hon. friends apposite, who were at the head of the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
government, express any fear as to the working of the theory of equality with regard to minorities or any other sections of the Canadian people.
May I remark that in all these discussions which took place the statesmen of Great Britain and the empire referred to history and emphasized the fact that the present organization of the empire and the problems of government which it presents cannot be understood unless they are studied in the light of historical development. Not only is it the result of a long historical growth, but it is dependent on unwritten conferences, delicate adjustments and slowly established practice. It follows that it is not only not the law or the written documents which must be consulted, but also history and the understanding and the ideas of the people, and the meaning of the outward forms of our institutions. One of the great features, I believe, of the report is that which affects the king. The king is recognized more than before as the keystone of the structure of the empire. He becomes the head of each state of the commonwealth in a more intimate and national sense. As a result of this his position is probably more secure than ever. Whoever directs the affairs in Great Britain, whatever government is called to power in Great Britain, will see to it that the only bond which keeps the various nations of the empire together is permanently retained. The moment that republicanism has overthrown many of the thrones of Europe the British monarchy has got to increase its prestige. The crown centralizes the common ideas and the common traditions of the commonwealth. In this connection may I quote some words of His Royal Highness, the Prince of Wales, in one of his public utterances:
The king, as the constitutional sovereign of the empire, occupies exactly the same place in Canada and in the whole British Empire as he does in Great Britain, and his house, although originally founded in Great Britain, belongs equally to all the other nations of the commonwealth.
Mr. Speaker, I have dealt perhaps too extensively with this school of critics who claim that a big change was brought about by the conference. I will now deal with the other school which says nothing was done. I will point out some of the things which the conference did, not for the purpose, as I have already said, of creating a new status, but of harmonizing the existing conditions with the
principle universally adopted and recognized. I will deal briefly then with the subject from three standpoints, the political, the legislative and the judicial. In the political field some modifications have been agreed to regarding the form of treaty and the proceedings accompanying such treaty. I had the honour to be appointed chairman of the committee which was charged with the duty of considering all matters relating to treaties. This was a very important committee indeed, and its work was a difficult one, but I am pleased to say that a solution was found which was acceptable to all members of the committee. It is impossible for me to deal at length with this particular subject, but perhaps I may mention what the practice in future will be as a result of the work of the committee. Hereafter treaties will be made and signed, not by and for the British Empire, but by and for Great Britain and such other portions of the empire as may be concerned in those treaties. Heretofore, even though we might be interested in any treaty of any description, if we were not represented during its negotiation and at the signing of it, the treaty was entered into nevertheless in the name of the British Empire as a whole. The change in the wording of the treaty in this regard is of the utmost importance. There will be no longer any need of the provision which has been known as the exclusion clause, such for instance as was incorporated in the Locarno treaty. That clause was to the effect that the treaty in question could be enforced in any of the dominions only after they had agreed to come within its provisions. Such a clause, as I say, will no longer be necessary; it will serve no useful purpose for the reason that we shall be involved in any treaty only if we are a party thereto. Treaties will be made by the king not in the name, not of the British Empire but on behalf of Great Britain and whatever other section of the empire may be a participant in and a signatory to the negotiations.
Another important change concerns the appointment of plenipotentiaries representing the king in connection with negotiations leading up to treaties and the signing of those treaties. When a few years ago I was appointed plenipotentiary to negotiate a treaty with the United States it was stated by constitutional writers that no real change had been made inasmuch as my appointment by His Majesty the king was the outcome of an order in council passed by the Imperial government.
1706	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
The same with regard to the issuance of powers and the ratification that must take place after the signing of a treaty. That ratification was also made by His Majesty the king upon an order in council of the Imperial government and not of the Canadian government, even where Canada was concerned. Now treaties signed on behalf of Canada will be signed by a plenipotentiary appointed by His Majesty the king upon a recommendation of the Canadian government, and the issuance of powers will be made also upon the recommendation of the government of Canada. In the same way the ratification of treaties will be carried out upon the recommendation of the government of this Dominion. All the other formalities which, according to constitutional writers, have been adhered to as symbolic of the unity of the empire have been discarded as being no longer in harmony with the conditions now prevailing among the nations of the empire; for, as I have pointed out, the one great symbol of unity now is His Majesty the King. Let me observe that for this as for most of the other matters included in the report there is no need for any legislation; all that is needed is to harmonize the practice and usages with the present constitutional position of the dominions.
I come now to an objection raised yesterday by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that possibly we might now be tacitly involved in a treaty in which we had taken no part, by reason of the fact that we had not responded to the call of the government initiating the treaty. In consequence of the change that has been brought about, all the nations of the empire are on the same footing, and no treaty must necessarily be initiated by Great Britain. We in Canada have the right to initiate any treaty which concerns ourselves. If we initiate a treaty relating to matters in which some of the other dominions may have an interest, surely it is our duty to inform those dominions in that respect. Take for instance the case of a treaty which we might enter into with the United States with regard to the fisheries in the Atlantic in which Newfoundland would be concerned. Our duty, in accordance with the procedure that has been accepted, would be, before entering into negotiations, to inform Newfoundland of our intention to make a treaty with the United States in that matter, and if Newfoundland desired to join she would be free to do so. If, on the other hand, she did not answer-and only in that case- then undoubtedly we should be free to carry on our negotiations and Newfoundland could not complain. But there is a reservation: Newfoundland would not be in any way bound
[Mr. Lapointe.l
should the treaty in any way involve her in active obligations. In such a case Newfoundland, or any other dominion for that matter, although she might not have responded, although she might have neglected to declare her position in the matter after being informed of the intention of the Canadian government to enter into negotiations, would not be involved in any active obligation as a consequence of the making of that treaty. Even here the principle of the equality of status is confirmed more markedly than it was before because, as I have stated, we are all on an equal footing. If a treaty concerns us we have the right to initiate it and we inform Great Britain or any other part of the empire of our intentions in the matter if they are interested therein.

speechtext: Just how far does the principle of equality of status extend? Does it extend, for example, to treaties involving assistance in the event of war?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

No, I am sure it does
not, and this by reason of these words:
It must, however, before taking any steps which might involve the other governments in any active obligations, obtain their definite assent.
In any case where any other government may be involved in active obligations-and the hon. member is referring to a case in which there would be such obligations-then the definite assent of the government involved must be given.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Is this the implication of the minister's remarks, that Canada in future will hold a neutral position unless she has given her assent to participation in such a treaty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
The discussion of that
phase of the matter would lead me into a long argument.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
But it is so
essential.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I say that Canada will always be free to take whatever steps she thinks fit. She will not be bound to any active obligation.
Now, as to foreign affairs, the outstanding feature of the report is, I believe, the definite recognition that neither Great Britain nor the dominions are committed to any active obligations except with the assent of their own governments or parliaments. It is stated clearly in the report. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) yesterday invited me to speak of the Locarno treaty, owing to the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
fact that some one had made reference to it in the British House of Commons. If my hon. friend reads the resolution in the report, as I am sure he has done many times, he will see that it is merely an expression of congratulation to the Foreign Secretary of England for the part he took in trying to bring about peace in Europe. I do not think I am betraying any secret when I say that we have taken the position that we are not bound by the Locarno treaty, which was initiated and entered into by the British government without the cooperation of Canada. I have no criticism to offer in that -respect; it was largely a matter of concern to the government of Great Britain, and was a European matter. As I have seen it expressed in the newspapers of this country, we may be bound to some extent if there is a war between the nations which are signatories to the treaty; we may have some obligation on account of our -membership in the British commonwealth of nations and as members of the -League of Nations, but our obligations as British subjects and as members of the League of Nations are quite different from the obligations which we would assume if we were to guarantee the boundaries between France and Germany, thus assuming obligations with regard to foreign powers at a distance of over 3,000 miles from the limits of Canada. I think we have exactly the same reason for not entering into that treaty as Great Britain had when she refused to give the same guarantee to the eastern boundary of Germany as she gave to the western boundary. The eastern boundaries of Germany touch on Poland, and in that connection the British government refused to sign any guarantee. That guarantee was signed by France, but the British government refused to be involved in the question of -the boundaries on the eastern side of Germany because they were too remote, and the same reason would apply with us so far as the western boundary is concerned. So I may say to the hon. member for Lafoelle that Canada has not ratified the pact of Locarno and is not a party to it.
The change with regard to the Governor General also comes under this heading of political modifications. The Governor General is no longer in any respect an officer of the Imperial government; he has virtually the position of a viceroy, having the same prerogatives and powers as His Majesty the King. He is no longer a channel of communication, as he formerly was, and although in this country I have heard and read that this was not a change, the gentlemen representing Britain who signed the report had a different conception, because they state in the report that it is a change.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
May I ask a question?
Was not the same thing agreed to at the conference which Sir Robert Borden attended?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
I answered that question before it was asked. Indeed, it was a change going much deeper than most people realized. Heretofore the Governor General, notwithstanding what was stated to the con-t-arary, was the representative of the British government, as well as the representative of the king. He acted as a channel of communication between the governments of Great Britain and the dominion; he represented to the Dominion government the wishes of the British government, and kept the British government in touch with the views of the Dominion executive. There was certainly something anomalous in the position of a Governor General who was bound to accept the advice of his ministers but who was at the same time informing another government of the policies and the wishes of those same ministers. It may be that it is important, and I think it is, that the British government should be represented in Canada as Canada is represented in the capital of the empire, but the British government must and should be represented by an official who would not be the representative of the king and who would not be the Governor General of Canada.
So far as the legislative sphere is concerned, it is in some respects difficult to harmonize the principle of equality with existing conditions and with special situations which have to be considered. Here is what the report says with regard to the general principle covering the matter:
On this point we propose that it should be placed on record that, apart from provisions embodied in constitutions or in specific statutes expressly providing for reservation, it is recognized that it is the right of the government of each dominion to advise the crown in all matters relating to its own affairs. Consequently, it would not be in accordance with constitutional practice for advice to be tendered to His Majesty by His Majesty's government in Great Britain in any matter appertaining to the affairs of a dominion against the views of the government of that dominion.
The appropriate procedure with regard to projected legislation in one of the self-governing parts of the empire -which may affect the interests of other self-governing parts is previous consultation between His Majesty's ministers in the several parts concerned.
The points on which there seems to be a conflict with the doctrine of equality are very few. They are the powers of disallowance and in some cases reservation of dominion legislation, the doubt as to the powers of the dominion legislatures to enact laws having to do with extra-territorial jurisdiction, and
1708	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
more particularly the provisions of the Colonial Laws Validity Act of 1865. Nothing definite has been suggested in the report as to the change which should be made with regard to these subjects, but the conference has recommended that a committee of legal experts should be appointed by Great Britain and the representatives of the dominions to inquire into the whole matter and make recommendations that would safeguard all interests and still agree with the general principle laid down by the conference.
I will deal briefly with each one of these subjects. I am glad everyone who has so far taken part in the debate, even my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, has agreed that the power of dissallowance is obsolete and can be said at present to have no constitutional effect. Indeed, Sir Robert Borden used very strong language in that regard, when he said that this power is constitutionally dead. There are, however, in the constitutions of some dominions, matters which have to be reserved for the assent of the king in order to protect certain particular interests. Foil instance, laws affecting alterations of the powers of the states of the Commopwealth :odj Australia have to be reserved for the assent of the king under the constitution of Australia; laws affecting the constitution or powers of the provincial councils of South Africa and certain acts of the lower house there must also be reserved. All these features would1 have to be considered by the committee of legal experts.
Perhaps at this stage I might say something about the rights of the various dominions to change their own constitutions. I have already had occasion, even during the present session, to refer to the British North America Act, and to give the reasons why in that constitution power was not given to the Dominion of Canada to alter it. Confederation was a compromise. The provinces agreed to give up some of their powers and entrust them to the federal authority, while taking to themselves certain other powers, and within the limits of their jurisdiction they are as supreme and they have just as many rights of selfgovernment as the Dominion of Canada has within its own jurisdiction. The power of altering the constitution was not given in the British North America Act because of the circumstances of this country, to which I need not refer. In Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and the Irish Free State they have this power of modifying their own constitution, but not to as large an extent as some people seem to think.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Except Australia.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: Australia? Well, some of the states of Australia cannot-

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: I mean the commonwealth.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: The commonwealth itself has wide powers, but they have to be exercised by absolute majorities in both houses of parliament and approved on referendum by the electors; and every time any change with regard to the relations between, the commonwealth and the states of Australia has been sought that change has always been defeated when the referendum went to the people. In New Zealand some important constitutional changes would have to be reserved for the royal assent. In South Africa changes affecting the number and distribution of seats in the lower house, the native franchise in the Cape province, and equality of the Dutch and English languages can be brought about only by two-thirds majority of both houses at a joint sitting.

subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext: After ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE
speechtext:
Yes, after ten years,
and as I said before, changes affecting the provinces of South Africa have to be reserved for the assent of the king. In this country, as I have already stated, the provinces are autonomous in their own sphere. The crown acts with regard to provincial matters upon the advice of the government of the province. As I had occasion to state in other circumstances, when we speak of the autonomy of Canada we speak of Canada as the confederation of nine provinces, each one of those provinces having as supreme powers within its own sphere as the federal authority here has with respect to its sphere. May I quote here the words of Sir Robert Borden in the House of Commons in a speech delivered in 1917 with regard to the crown acting upon the advice of the provinces in those matters:
The crown acts in the United Kingdom and in all the self-governing dominions of the empire, it acts in the United Kingdom upon the advice of the ministers of the United Kingdom, it acts in each of the dominions upon the ad-vice_ of the appropriate ministers-in federal affairs, upon the advice of federal ministers; in provincial and state affairs, upon the advice of provincial and state ministers. It is the same crown throughout, acting upon the advice of different ministers. That tie of allegiance to the crown is the tie which chiefly binds together the empire to-day so far as constitutional considerations are concerned.
The language of the report preserves the right of the provinces which are absolutely self-governing in those matters coming within their jurisdiction. The principle of equality

Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
is not, I submit, affected by such condition, which is merely the expression of the will of the people.
Many people claim that the fact that we cannot in this parliament alter our own constitution is creating a state of subordination.
I claim that so long as this condition exists because of the will of the Canadian people, a condition which will exist as long as the Canadian people wish it to do so, changes that could be made shall have to be made by the parties to the contract. But that condition, which is dependent upon our own wish in the matter, does not, I claim, create a state of subordination. I deny most emphatically that a condition of subordination and colonial inferiority is essential to the preservation of the rights of minorities in Canada. And let me tell the leader of the opposition that those for whom I claim I have some right to speak, have always fought for responsible government and for selfgovernment in this country, for freedom and national status within the British Empire and under the British crown.
As I have already stated, the report of the conference does not and could not in any way modify the pact of confederation. The courts have decided both ways. At times the Privy Council has decided in favour of granting that right to the dominion, and at other times it has denied that right to the dominion. The courts in the dominions themselves have also not been unanimous in that respect. We in Canada have always claimed that we have that right. In 1920 the president of the Air Board asked this government to take the necessary steps to make it clear that legislation or regulations concerning aviation would follow Canadian subjects even after they had crossed over the boundary line. We have the same complication with regard to customs matters. It seems necessary for Canada that Canadian subjects who, for instance, conspire outside the limits of this country to defraud the public treasury, should be amenable to the laws of the land. And further there is this fine language in the order in council:
In the growth of the constitution the United Kingdom and the dominions have under His Majesty relations which may be assimilated to those nf independent sovereign states-

The work of the Imperial conference of 1926 has been accepted everywhere, not only in Great Britain but -in the dominions, as having been of great value. It is commended in all quarters. I should like to have the time to quote many expressions of opinion in that regard, for even men who went there far from being satisfied left with a sense of satisfaction which means something to those who have at heart the preservation of the empire. Here is what General Hertzog said before leaving London:
I feel that nothing has ever before been accomplished so calculated to lay a deep and enduring foundation for national cooperation between members of the British commonwealth of nations and insure real good feeling between us all.
A very influential American newspaper, the Washington Post, commenting on the conference, wrote:
It may be observed that if the government of George III had possessed the wdsdom of the government of George V, there would have been no declaration of independence, and the United States would now be part of the British commonwealth. Mr. Amery, who I need not say is a strong imperialist, has the following to say:
The conference marks the acknowledged coming-of-age of the younger nations of our commonwealth, and that is a great fact in history which it is worth while pausing a moment to recall. I think the time will undoubtedly come when the growth of the younger British

nations in the bosom of the British commonwealth will be recognized to have been at least as great an event in the history of the world as the coming into existence of other nations during the last fifty or sixty years which have attracted much more public attention, because they have come into existence as the result of wars, whether rvars that have led to unity, as in the case of the coming into existence of the united Italy or the united Germany, or wars which have broken up older organizations, as those which have created the new countries of central and north-eastern Europe. . . . What it does mean is that each partner in the empire is equally entitled to exercise every function of national life, and if any such function is carried on for it by some other part of the empire, that is a matter of consent, of convenience, of mutual arrangement, and not evidence of subordination on the part of one partner in the empire to another.
In this country, unfortunately, the situation is not what it is in Great Britain and some of the other dominions of the empire. Before I commit myself may I be allowed to quote certain words from an important periodical in this country, the Dalhousie Review,-all the more important, perhaps, in that the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Ben-nett) is numbered among its directors. At the conclusion of a very clever and significant article on the work of the Imperial conference the writer says:

This is the first time in Canada, as I believe it is the first time in the history of the British commonwealth of -nations, that an amendment has been moved in the shape of the one submitted in this instance, and speeches have been delivered outside of parliament such as have -been made in this connection, as a result of the work of an Imperial conference. subtopic: DEBATE ON STATEMENT OF PRIME MINISTER AND AMENDMENT OF MR. GUTHRIE

speechtext: I have no complaint to make about free discussion, but I think the amendment goes a little further than free discussion; and I say that my hon. friends of the Conservative party, by the voice of their leader and the moving of this amendment, have sounded the first discordant note in the British commonwealth with regard to the Imperial conference. Are they sincere? Is my hon. friend sincere? As I have said, never before was any motion introduced in parliament such as the one now proposed, and my hon. friend never before protested against such a course as we are now following. Do hon. gentlemen think that they help to preserve the empire by adopting such an attitude? Do they think they are adding to the value of the Imperial conference? Last fall after the general elections, which I believe were held on September 14,-the conference was to open in London in October-views were advanced that under the circumstances Canada could abstain from attending the conference: it was an arduous undertaking for men who had been during the course of two years in the thick of a political fight which we all recollect. Conservative newspapers and Conservative public men expressed the view in no uncertain terms that it was the duty of the government returned to power to attend that conference; it was a sacred duty, and we would have been strongly and bitterly criticized if we had not done so. If he will permit me to say so, I believe in my modest way that I am just as able to protect those interests as he is. I believe it is not fair;
I believe it is not conducive to empire building, and I believe that if Canadian public men must face that kind of warfare perhaps some of them might very well come to the opinion already held by others that they should not attend these conferences but should look for the settlement of Canadian questions on this side of the water, by Canadians and in this country only. That is where my hon. friends are leading with the warfare they are now waging, and I claim it is not fair.
Mr. Speaker, the rights of the minorities in Canada and the rights of the minority in Quebec can, I believe, be safeguarded by myself quite as well as by the leader of the opposition. He is afraid for the future, and for those who will come fifty or one hundred years from now; let him unite with me to correct the present evils instead of looking so far ahead. This is not a fair way to conduct political warfare on a question of this kind. I do not wish to say more in that regard, but I resented very much and still resent the implications contained in the speech of the leader of the opposition and in the amendment which he brought forward. I have done my duty, and I think I can still do my duty.
I know this attempt will be futile, however, and I will forget it altogether in order to bring my remarks to a more pleasant and happy conclusion. There is no such thing as an indefinite status quo in national life; populations grow, conditions of life change, and it is the part of wisdom for governments to legislate for present and future requirements. The British Empire is composed of men of almost every race; it includes nations developing their destinies under various racial, economic and political conditions peculiar to themselves. In our membership we have elements which, outside of the empire, would often lead to war, but the aim is to evolve a system by which various interests, even though at first sight they may seem opposed and antagonistic, may be coordinated in such a manner that individual national sentiments and industrial and economic development may be fully promoted and encouraged by the

Imperial Conference-Mr. Lapointe
various means and policies best suited to the respective peoples, at the same time engendering sympathy and good feeling towards one another. Such was the spirit which animated the men who took part in the conference of 1926. The British Empire has been founded and is maintained on and by compromise. There could not be a more striking illustration of that than to see a Dutchman from South Africa, a Frenchman from Canada and an Irishman from the Free State meeting on an equal footing with the public men of Great Britain, and cooperating with them in an endeavour to find the best mode of preserving the association of our nations.
We are celebrating this year the sixtieth anniversary of confederation; the work of building a nation in Canada has been achieved, and no more evidence of that fact is needed than the debate which is now proceeding. We may say with pride that on the whole the task of the statesmen of 1867 has been successful. Our country', as well as the British commonwealth of nations, is founded on compromise. There may be some who are impatient for changes in the pact which was agreed upon in 1867, and I would be the last to suggest that some modifications might not be made which would improve conditions. I fully agree that the problems of 1927 must be settled in the light of conditions which exist in 1927; that the questions of to-day must not be settled as they would have been settled by the men who lived sixty years ago, but as they would have been settled had those men been living to-day. But certain essen-tional and inherent conditions of our national existence require the greatest care and prudence in their study, and whatever suggestions may be considered the basis of the pact of confederation must be maintained at least in so far as our internal affairs are concerned. Sir, the principles and fundamental ideals which underlie that' pact are the fuel necessary that the torch may burn brighter and illuminate through the darkness of our conflicts and difficulties the road to peace, progress and nationhood in this country.

This country comprises half a continent. Our population numbers nine millions of people. We have resources available to us such as no other population of like number in the wide world possess to-day. We have problems of every kind and description-political, social, educational and industrial-to solve for the great advantage of the country to-day, and for its material and moral prosperity and progress in the future. Therefore we on this side are as strong nationalists in all that pertains to the development of Canada and its national life as were our predecessors-Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Thompson, or any other of the old leaders of the Conservative party to whom the minister made reference this afternoon. But we on this side, and the party which we represent throughout the country, do conceive that the best aspirations and traditions of the two great races that originally founded the Canadian confederacy-and the men of all other races who have come in and declared themselves brothers of the blood with us in building up and developing Canada will find this to be the case-that we are true to our best traditions, that we will be carrying out our highest and best ideals, that we will best ensure the integrity and stability of this country for all time, by maintaining our political unity, not only with the British crown but with Great Britain and the other dominions beyond the seas; and whatever difficulties and problems we may encounter in working along that line, I say that the end to be attained is far more consistent with our best traditions of the past, is far more honourable to the two great races in Canada, than to form any other conceivable connection with any other political power for the purpose of securing our national defence and the maintenance of the integrity of this country.
